trace.topic: SaaS Isn’t Dead. But the Way You Used to Win in B2B? That’s Gone.
trace.goal: Argue that the category still matters but the old growth playbook has broken.
expected_facts: The answer should reject the simplistic claim that SaaS is dead.
It should argue that the historical playbook has changed materially.
It should explain how founders need to adapt in product, GTM, or capital strategy.
rubric_must_haves: Makes the distinction between category health and playbook change explicit.
Explains what has changed and why.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that SaaS remains a huge and important category, but the old easy-growth playbook no longer works the same way. Founders now need sharper product differentiation, better efficiency, and more disciplined execution. The lesson is not despair; it is adaptation.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: SaaS Isn’t Dead. But the Way You Used to Win in B2B? That’s Gone.

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.

[E16] Twilio is now above 10% growth again.
[E17] Salesforce has seen a boost.

trace.answer:
SaaS isn’t dead. Not yet.  Even though times are still tougher than the go-go years of 2021.
But the playbook everyone used to win?  Yeah, it’s mostly gone. Or at least, in many cases, under pressure.  So far, most public SaaS companies haven’t seen any downturn, although they have seen deceleration in growth.  And startups are finding things harder than ever.  Especially those without an incredible product tailwind.
The reason isn’t demand. Software budgets are still going up. CIOs need more AI agents, more tools, more software to run their operations. More. The budget is there. The headcount is there. The urgency is there.
What’s different now is that every startup selling to enterprises faces exactly the same thing. Every one. Not because they’re similar products—they’re not—but because buyers are fundamentally changing their behavior across categories. The shift from people to per-conversation pricing for AI tools. The desire for plug-and-play solutions instead of complex implementations. The expectation of instant ROI rather than gradual improvement.
The market doesn’t reward mediocrity anymore. The gap between excellent and mediocre has grown exponentially. Why? Because AI has given us options. Buyers have options. For decades, once you got past the evaluation phase, you had roughly three choices: keep using whatever you already paid for, switch to another solution you’ve also bought, or stay with the original provider because switching costs were real.
Those options feel quaint compared to what exists today. Now buyers can choose between dozens of vendors with comparable capabilities, each with their own unique strengths and weaknesses. And they’re choosing fast—often within weeks, sometimes overnight.
For founders who grew up building traditional SaaS businesses, this creates existential anxiety.

SaaS isn’t dead. Not yet. It still grows at epic rates. But it’s very different than it used to be. And for many of us, the game has changed. What hasn’t changed:
The underlying demand for software remains enormous
AI is accelerating the pace of work and driving productivity gains across industries
Companies continue to need solutions to solve real problems
Budgets remain available for technology investments
The fundamentals of building a successful business haven’t disappeared
What HAS fundamentally changed:
How quickly markets evolve and disrupt each other
How fast competition emerges and scales
Customer expectations around automation and integration
The speed at which technologies become commoditized
The ability to maintain competitive advantages
And one thing that hasn’t changed in years …
is the #1 reason deals fail
. We’ve talked about this over and over and over on SaaStr since Day One. In the end, every SaaS sale fails because the buyer doesn’t believe the product will deliver the ROI promised by the seller. This hasn’t changed. At least not that much. And yet … most founders still think it’s 2010/2020. Most founders still think customers pick vendors like they did in the past. That’s why folks are confused these days. Folks are seeing seemingly identical products being priced out of market. Why would a customer pay 50%-100% more for what seems to be the same exact solution? Because … they didn’t use to. Even though prices went up significantly from 2011 to 2021. What they used to do instead was try harder. They had fewer choices, so they worked hard to figure out who was best. So they chose whoever they believed could deliver the highest ROI, given the budget constraints. If they couldn’t decide between two vendors, they usually picked the one with the higher likelihood of success.

retrieval_hits.text:
SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

So it was just 8 months ago
we wrote “Is SaaS Dead?
” and the post not only took off, it summarized a zeitgeist, a malaise, a feeling across much of B2B at the start of 2024. That SaaS was Dead. A combination of AI and buyer retrenchment had killed it. What a difference 8 months makes. It’s not 2021 again, but so much has changed for the better as the year ends:
Many top SaaS and Cloud stocks are up +40%-60% or more in the back half of the yea
r. Not all of them, but so many. This makes everyone feel … richer. They are richer. Many top SaaS and Cloud leaders have seen growth re-accelerate
. This is a bigger deal. Shopify is growing far faster today at $9B ARR (a stunning 26%) than it was just a year before (21%). Even folks that were struggling to rebound from pandemic-fueled growth like Twilio have bounced back, to an extent at least. Twilio is now above 10% growth again. This isn’t 2020 levels of growth, but acceleration is acceleration. Many SaaS leaders are now benefitting from selling AI
. Salesforce has seen a boost. Dialpad has seen
stunning re-acceleration, from $200m ARR last year to $300m+ this year
. Not everyone has benefitted from selling AI to their base. But a number have. IPOs are restarting — and really good ones are coming
. There have only been 4 SaaS IPOs since 2021, but they’ve done well, and ServiceTitan had a big pop in its recent IPO. The pipeline looks strong for the back half of 2025 and into 2026, from Canva to Databricks to Stripe to Wiz to Snyk and on and on. More liquidity makes everyone feel better, for many reasons.
New!!  There Probably Is No Downturn in SaaS. It’s Time To Stop Waiting For It To End.

Topic: SaaS Isn’t Dead. But the Way You Used to Win in B2B? That’s Gone.

Source passages:
[train_12669]
SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

[train_5411]
The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

[train_6660]
So it was just 8 months ago
we wrote “Is SaaS Dead?
” and the post not only took off, it summarized a zeitgeist, a malaise, a feeling across much of B2B at the start of 2024. That SaaS was Dead. A combination of AI and buyer retrenchment had killed it. What a difference 8 months makes. It’s not 2021 again, but so much has changed for the better as the year ends:
Many top SaaS and Cloud stocks are up +40%-60% or more in the back half of the yea
r. Not all of them, but so many. This makes everyone feel … richer. They are richer. Many top SaaS and Cloud leaders have seen growth re-accelerate
. This is a bigger deal. Shopify is growing far faster today at $9B ARR (a stunning 26%) than it was just a year before (21%). Even folks that were struggling to rebound from pandemic-fueled growth like Twilio have bounced back, to an extent at least. Twilio is now above 10% growth again. This isn’t 2020 levels of growth, but acceleration is acceleration. Many SaaS leaders are now benefitting from selling AI
. Salesforce has seen a boost. Dialpad has seen
stunning re-acceleration, from $200m ARR last year to $300m+ this year
. Not everyone has benefitted from selling AI to their base. But a number have. IPOs are restarting — and really good ones are coming
. There have only been 4 SaaS IPOs since 2021, but they’ve done well, and ServiceTitan had a big pop in its recent IPO. The pipeline looks strong for the back half of 2025 and into 2026, from Canva to Databricks to Stripe to Wiz to Snyk and on and on. More liquidity makes everyone feel better, for many reasons.
